facts.label: Readiness view
facts.text: The source set is adequate for the requested snapshot, with bounded limitations. Every section the later analysis needs is present in text form in the filed statements: income statement, balance sheet and cash flow for FY2025 and for each 2026 quarter, the debt note, the liquidity discussion with the revolver and covenant summary, segment tables, and the legal and subsequent-event disclosures. Filed statements and the audited annual report control; the three earnings releases are attributed management claims and agree with the filings on every tied figure. The strongest contrary evidence is not a conflict but an absence: the executed credit agreement, its February 2026 amendment and the indentures are listed in the annual report exhibit index but are not in the pinned set, no actual covenant ratio is printed, no letter-of-credit usage figure is printed, and rating information is limited to one annual-report sentence. The mechanism is that covenant definitions and headroom, revolver availability net of letters of credit, and note guarantor structure then rest on filer summaries rather than executed terms, so any later covenant or liquidity-headroom statement must be labelled as a summary-based limitation. Nothing in the set is blocked. No document dated after the cutoff is used. The next evidence action, if the committee needs covenant headroom, is to add the executed credit agreement, first amendment and the five note indentures, and the compliance figures or rating agency reports.

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The financial base is well supported for reported facts and weaker for derived credit metrics. Reported facts: Molina is a managed-care payer whose earnings compressed sharply as the medical care ratio (MCR, medical costs over premium revenue) rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026, so that operating income fell from 1,707 in FY2024 to 781 in FY2025 and to 334 in 9M 2026 against 943 in 9M 2025. Debt is five parent-level senior unsecured notes with 3,800 of principal and 3,771 of carrying value at September 30, 2026, no amount drawn on the 1,250 revolver, and no principal due before June 2028. Calculated metrics, not reported by the company: EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization) was 1,893 in FY2024, 976 in FY2025 and 333 for the LTM to September 30, 2026, which puts total debt to EBITDA at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x. The mechanism is operating leverage on a fixed debt stack: debt did not fall while earnings did, and interest expense rose from 118 in FY2024 to 192 in FY2025 after the November 2024 and November 2025 note issuances and the 2025 term loan borrowings. Interest expense over the LTM to September 30, 2026 was 213, so EBITDA over interest expense is 1.56x on this simple basis, below the 1.75 to 1.00 covenant floor in force through December 31, 2026. That comparison is not a covenant test: the credit agreement defines the ratio and the sources do not print the definition or the reported ratio, the company states it is in compliance (10-Q Q3 page:15), and adding back the 93 non-cash impairment alone lifts the simple ratio to 2.00x. The consolidated balance sheet shows net cash (consolidated cash and equivalents of 4,479 exceed debt of 3,771), but most of that cash supports claims and statutory capital at the regulated health plans, so the parent view (608 of cash and investments) is the better liquidity guide for debt service. Near-term maturity pressure is limited because no principal falls due before June 2028, so the credit question is earnings recovery and covenant headroom rather than refinancing in the next year. What the evidence supports: the reported statements, debt table, maturities, revolver size and parent cash. What it restricts: any statement of covenant headroom, cash-interest coverage for the latest twelve months, or revolver availability net of letters of credit. The context holds no ratings, so the only rating evidence is the annual report sentence that each senior note is rated BB by S&P and Ba2 by Moody's (10-K page:94).

facts.text: - Earnings pressure is margin-driven, not revenue-driven at the premium line in 2025: premium revenue rose from 38,627 to 43,052 in FY2025 while medical margin fell from 4,199 to 3,564 (10-K page:81). In 2026 premium revenue also fell (30,873 in 9M 2026 against 32,337), mainly on lower Medicaid and Marketplace membership (Q3 release page:1), so both a lower revenue base and a higher MCR now weigh on earnings. Marketplace MCR was 90.6% in FY2025 against 75.4% in FY2024 (10-K page:85). - The fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss on a derived basis: FY2025 operating income of 781 less 9M 2025 of 943 gives -162 (see Calculations). That quarter is what lifts the LTM interest-cover measure down to 1.56x. - Leverage view by balance sheet: debt to capital on a simple basis (debt over debt plus equity) is 47.58% at September 30, 2026, against 48.07% at December 31, 2025 and 39.40% at December 31, 2024. The covenant maximum is 60% (65% for four quarters after a material acquisition), defined by the credit agreement; the simple ratio is indicative only. - Claims outside debt: medical claims and benefits payable of 4,988 and amounts due government agencies of 1,141 at September 30, 2026 are operating liabilities outside the debt figure (10-Q Q3 page:2). Finance lease liabilities were 209 in total at December 31, 2025 (25 current, 184 non-current) and operating lease liabilities 71 (10-K page:127); both are outside the debt figure. Pensions, factoring and supply-chain finance: none found in the sources (searched). - Liquidity depends on subsidiary dividends: regulated subsidiaries paid 985 in 2025 and 997 in 2024 to the parent (10-K page:90); for 9M 2026 the parent received 329 in dividends and return of capital and contributed 130 of capital (10-Q Q3 page:35). Dividends payable without regulatory approval were about 170 in aggregate at December 31, 2025, and the company expected a decline in such dividends for 2026 (10-K page:94). Minimum statutory capital and surplus was about 3.1 billion at December 31, 2025 (10-K page:93). - Capital return and financing: 1,000 of common stock was purchased in FY2025 and none in 9M 2026; 500 remained authorized through December 31, 2026 as of October 16, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:40). In FY2025 the company borrowed 1,100 under the credit facility and term loans and repaid 1,100, and issued the 850 6.500% notes in November 2025 with net proceeds of 838 (10-K page:107). - Latest quarter and subsequent events to the cutoff: the Q3 release reaffirmed FY2026 guidance (premium revenue of approximately $42 billion; GAAP earnings of at least $2.38 per diluted share; adjusted earnings of at least $5.25), including a loss of $1.50 per share from implementing the new Florida Medicaid contract in Q4 2026 and $1.00 from traditional MAPD (Q3 release page:2). The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:18). The Q3 2026 debt note (10-Q Q3 pages 14-15) shows the same five notes as December 31, 2025 and no drawing on the revolver; no debt issuance or further amendment after February 4, 2026 appears in the pinned sources. - Covenant facts: minimum interest coverage 3.0 to 1.0, reduced by the February 4, 2026 amendment to 1.75 to 1.00 for quarters ending March 31, 2026 to December 31, 2026, then 2.00 (March 2027), 2.50 (June 2027) and 2.75 (September 2027); maximum Consolidated Total Debt to Capital Ratio 60% (10-Q Q3 page:15). facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a listed, sponsor-free managed-care organisation that "provides managed healthcare services under the Medicaid and Medicare programs, and through the state insurance marketplaces" (10-K, page:108), operating in 21 states with about 4.9 million members at September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3, page:5). Its customers are government payers ("Our primary customers are state Medicaid agencies and the federal government", 10-Q Q3, page:31), so revenue is a fixed per-member-per-month premium that the health plan underwrites against medical cost, and the credit mechanism is the gap between rate updates (set annually by states and CMS) and medical cost trend. That gap is the central fact of the period: the 10-K describes a "rate and trend imbalance that we believe to be temporary" (page:86), the medical care ratio rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026 (CP-1), and earnings compressed accordingly (CP-1 operating income, EBITDA and leverage). The business is concentrated: Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue (page:15), four state contracts (California, New York, Texas, Washington) each exceed 10% of Medicaid premium revenue, and Medicaid contracts run three to five years with either side able to terminate with or without cause (page:108), so each re-procurement is a revenue-durability event (Virginia was lost: contracts terminated June 30, 2025, page:12). Two portfolio actions are reshaping 2026 and 2027: the Marketplace book is being cut deliberately (9M 2026 Marketplace premium revenue 1,994 against 3,401, membership 267,000 against 713,000, 10-Q Q3 pages 31-34) and the traditional Medicare Advantage-Part D product will be exited for 2027 with a 93 impairment recognized in Q1 2026 (CP-1). Management's long-term growth targets (premium revenue growth of 11% to 13% and passing $50 billion in 2027, 10-K page:10) are Management Language and sit against FY2026 premium revenue guidance of approximately $42 billion, so they are not used as a base case. No sponsor, controlling holder, dividend recapitalisation or related-party leakage appears in the sources; the documented capital-allocation behaviour is a pattern of share repurchases funded by subsidiary dividends, assessed below as Neutral or Mixed. Debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes plus an undrawn revolver (CP-1); whether subsidiaries guarantee the notes is not stated in the sources. The evidence supports a business and transaction read at the level of Documentary Facts; it restricts conclusions on ownership, control rights and covenant capacity because the proxy-based ownership information and executed documents are not supplied.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: New debt and facilities (Documentary Fact, status: completed). On November 20, 2025 the company completed a private offering of $850 million of 6.500% senior notes due February 15, 2031, with interest payable semiannually on February 15 and August 15 from August 15, 2026 and deferred issuance costs of $12 million; net proceeds repaid $740 million of term loan debt under the prior credit agreement and funded general corporate purposes (10-K page:131). The same day the company entered a new credit agreement replacing the June 8, 2020 agreement, with a $1.25 billion revolver terminating November 20, 2030, a $15 million swingline, a $100 million letter-of-credit sub-facility and uncommitted incremental term loans of up to $800 million for acquisitions (10-K page:131); Truist Bank is administrative agent (10-K page:153). Earlier, $750 million of 6.250% notes due January 15, 2033 were issued in November 2024 (10-K pages 83, 130). The February 4, 2026 First Amendment temporarily reduced the minimum interest coverage ratio to 1.75 to 1.00 for quarters through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters (10-K page:132); the amendment was agreed before the Q1 2026 reporting and is a subsequent event relative to the FY2025 balance sheet. During 2025 the company borrowed 950 of term loans and 150 under the credit facility and repaid all of them (10-K page:132). Liquidity effect: the notes refinanced the term loans and left the revolver undrawn; parent cash and investments are in CP-1. Use of proceeds, amounts and rates are stated in the filing; the executed indentures and credit agreement are not in the pinned set, so covenant baskets and restricted-payment capacity are Insufficient Information.

rows.label: Molina is a pure-play government-sponsored managed-care payer with no sponsor and 75% of FY2025 premium revenue from Medicaid. Credit risk turns on margin recovery, the Florida start-up and the 2027 exit of one Medicare product.
Medicaid was 75% of FY2025 premium revenue, and four state contracts (California, New York, Texas, Washington) each exceeded 10% of Medicaid premium revenue.
Medical costs outran rates: the consolidated medical care ratio was 92.1% in 9M 2026 against 90.8% in 9M 2025, and management calls 2026 the trough year for Medicaid margins.
Full-year guidance includes a $1.50 per share loss from the Florida contract start-up and a $1.00 loss from the Medicare product being exited for 2027.
The company repurchased $1,000 million of stock in FY2025 and none in 9M 2026; $500 million of authorization remains through December 31, 2026.
The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026, and the derivative action dismissal notice was filed on October 6, 2026.
Chief executive and chief financial officer

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a deteriorating credit with adequate near-term liquidity: debt of USD 3,771 million equals 11.32x EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against 1.54x in FY2024 [CP-1 leverage table]. The strongest support is structure and timing: the debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes, no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028, and the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn. The weakest point is earnings: the medical care ratio reached 92.1% in nine months 2026 against 90.8%, leaving LTM EBITDA of USD 333 million against interest expense of USD 213 million. The outcome depends on whether Medicaid rate updates restore margins before the interest coverage floor steps up in 2027, which the sources cannot confirm.

The outcome depends on whether Medicaid rate updates restore margins before the interest coverage floor steps up in 2027, which the sources cannot confirm.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The first finding is the speed of the earnings decline. Operating income fell from USD 1,707 million in FY2024 to USD 781 million in FY2025 and to a calculated USD 172 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, while debt stayed near USD 3,771 million, so calculated EBITDA of USD 1,893 million, USD 976 million and USD 333 million puts total debt at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x [CP-1 financials table]. The mechanism is a fixed premium rate set against a medical cost trend that outran it: the medical care ratio was 89.1% in FY2024, 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in nine months 2026, and the implied fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss of USD 162 million [CP-1 calculations]. Because debt did not fall, each point of margin lost translates directly into higher leverage. On the parent cash basis net debt is 9.50x EBITDA for the same twelve months. This is a calculated, Documentary Fact finding with high confidence in the inputs and medium confidence in the EBITDA definition, since the company reports no EBITDA.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The second finding is that covenant headroom, the question that matters most for creditors, cannot be measured. The credit agreement requires minimum interest coverage, which the February 4, 2026 amendment reduced from 3.0 to 1.0 to 1.75 to 1.00 through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters, and a maximum debt to capital ratio of 60%; the company states compliance at September 30, 2026 [CP-1 observations]. A simple EBITDA over interest expense measure is 1.56x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, or 2.00x with the USD 93 million non-cash impairment added back, but the agreement defines the ratio and that definition and the reported ratio are not supplied. The mechanism is that relief was taken in advance and the floor rises as the amendment expires; the implication is that earnings must recover materially during 2027 or relief must be extended, and a simple-basis shortfall is illustrated under Calculations. Confidence is low because the decisive figure is absent.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The third finding is that liquidity is adequate for debt service but sits at the parent. Consolidated cash and cash equivalents were USD 4,479 million at September 30, 2026, yet most of it supports claims and statutory capital at regulated health plans; parent cash and investments were USD 608 million against USD 223 million at December 31, 2025, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn, and no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028 [CP-1 liquidity and maturity tables]. Subsidiary dividends to the parent were USD 985 million in 2025 and the parent received USD 329 million of dividends and return of capital in nine months 2026, against an expected decline in dividends payable without approval [CP-1 observations]. The mechanism is that creditors rely on subsidiary distributions that fall when earnings fall and that the parent must fund statutory capital first, so the revolver is the real backstop; letters of credit drawn on it are not printed, so availability net of letters of credit is unconfirmed.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The fourth finding is the maturity and refinancing profile. The five senior notes total USD 3,800 million in principal: USD 800 million in 2028, USD 650 million in 2030, USD 850 million in 2031, USD 750 million in 2032 and USD 750 million in 2033, at an annual coupon of about USD 191.4 million, or 5.04% of principal. Recent issuance priced at 6.500% in November 2025 and 6.250% in November 2024, so any refinancing at current levels raises cost, while LTM interest expense of USD 213 million already consumes a large share of the USD 333 million of EBITDA. The implication is limited near-term refinancing pressure but little capacity to absorb a further earnings shock before 2028.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The fifth finding concerns business risk. Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue and four state contracts (California, New York, Texas and Washington) are about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue [CP-1A operating model]. Medicaid contracts run three to five years and either party may terminate, so re-procurement outcomes and annual rate setting drive revenue, and the Virginia contract loss shows the exposure. Management states that 2026 is the trough year for Medicaid margins and that recent rate updates are strong for 2027, which is Management Language that the results through the third quarter of 2026 do not yet support: the Medicaid medical care ratio was 93.0% in the third quarter against 92.0%. The sixth finding is that near-term earnings carry identified drags: guidance includes a loss of USD 1.50 per diluted share from the new Florida contract and a loss of USD 1.00 per diluted share from the Medicare product to be exited for 2027, and the GAAP guidance floor of USD 122 million net income implies only about USD 10 million for the fourth quarter. The sources conflict on the scale of the Florida contract (about 120,000 enrollees against USD 6 billion of annual premium revenue), so the size of that start-up cost cannot be verified [CP-1A conflicts].

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The seventh finding is capital allocation and governance. The company repurchased USD 1,000 million of stock in FY2025, paused repurchases in nine months 2026 and retains USD 500 million of authorization through December 31, 2026, which is an Analyst Interpretation of Neutral or Mixed behaviour: the pause is supportive, but the authorization is a possible call on parent cash. The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 and the derivative dismissal notice was filed on October 6, 2026, which removes an overhang. The only rating evidence is BB from S&P and Ba2 from Moody's as stated in the annual report.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. The first strength is a favourable maturity and liquidity structure: no principal is due before USD 800 million in June 2028, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn and runs to November 20, 2030, and parent cash and investments rose to USD 608 million from USD 223 million, so the debt can be serviced for some time even on thin earnings (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The second is an unsecured, single-issuer capital structure at the parent with no sponsor, no creditor-adverse transaction found and no dividend recapitalisation, which limits governance and structural-priming risk (Documentary Fact, CP-1A, with the caveat that indentures are not supplied). The third is an established government-programme franchise with recent state procurement wins and a large Medicaid base; the contract win record is a management claim and is tagged Management Language, but the wins themselves are documented (CP-1A). The fourth is the pause in share repurchases in nine months 2026 and the dismissal of the securities and derivative suits, which reduce competing calls on parent cash and a legal overhang (Documentary Fact, CP-1 and CP-1A). The fifth is that operating cash flow was positive in nine months 2026 at USD 629 million, giving an operating cash flow less capital expenditure figure of USD 535 million, although this reflects settlement timing (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1).

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Weaknesses. The first weakness is leverage on collapsed earnings: 11.32x total debt to EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026 against 1.54x in FY2024, with a simple EBITDA over interest expense of 1.56x (Documentary Fact for inputs, calculated, CP-1). The second is unverifiable covenant headroom against a floor that rises from 1.75 to 1.00 to 2.75 to 1.00 by September 2027 (Insufficient Information on the executed definition and ratio; the relief obtained in advance is an Analyst Interpretation of limited headroom). The third is dependence on subsidiary dividends and on consolidated cash that is largely tied to statutory capital, so the headline net cash position does not measure parent debt-service capacity (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1). The fourth is concentration in Medicaid and in four states, with short and terminable contracts and an unproven margin recovery (Documentary Fact and Management Language, CP-1A). The fifth is settlement-driven cash flow: operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 535 million in FY2025 and an inflow of USD 629 million in nine months 2026, so cash conversion is volatile (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The sixth is the identified 2026 and 2027 earnings drags from the Florida start-up and the Medicare exit, together with policy risk from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with the Florida contract size in conflict across the sources (Documentary Fact and conflict, CP-1A).

### Financial base view

The financial base is well supported for reported facts and weaker for derived credit metrics. Reported facts: Molina is a managed-care payer whose earnings compressed sharply as the medical care ratio (MCR, medical costs over premium revenue) rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026, so that operating income fell from 1,707 in FY2024 to 781 in FY2025 and to 334 in 9M 2026 against 943 in 9M 2025. Debt is five parent-level senior unsecured notes with 3,800 of principal and 3,771 of carrying value at September 30, 2026, no amount drawn on the 1,250 revolver, and no principal due before June 2028. Calculated metrics, not reported by the company: EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization) was 1,893 in FY2024, 976 in FY2025 and 333 for the LTM to September 30, 2026, which puts total debt to EBITDA at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x. The mechanism is operating leverage on a fixed debt stack: debt did not fall while earnings did, and interest expense rose from 118 in FY2024 to 192 in FY2025 after the November 2024 and November 2025 note issuances and the 2025 term loan borrowings. Interest expense over the LTM to September 30, 2026 was 213, so EBITDA over interest expense is 1.56x on this simple basis, below the 1.75 to 1.00 covenant floor in force through December 31, 2026. That comparison is not a covenant test: the credit agreement defines the ratio and the sources do not print the definition or the reported ratio, the company states it is in compliance (10-Q Q3 page:15), and adding back the 93 non-cash impairment alone lifts the simple ratio to 2.00x. The consolidated balance sheet shows net cash (consolidated cash and equivalents of 4,479 exceed debt of 3,771), but most of that cash supports claims and statutory capital at the regulated health plans, so the parent view (608 of cash and investments) is the better liquidity guide for debt service. Near-term maturity pressure is limited because no principal falls due before June 2028, so the credit question is earnings recovery and covenant headroom rather than refinancing in the next year. What the evidence supports: the reported statements, debt table, maturities, revolver size and parent cash. What it restricts: any statement of covenant headroom, cash-interest coverage for the latest twelve months, or revolver availability net of letters of credit. The context holds no ratings, so the only rating evidence is the annual report sentence that each senior note is rated BB by S&P and Ba2 by Moody's (10-K page:94).

### Credit-relevant observations

- Earnings pressure is margin-driven, not revenue-driven at the premium line in 2025: premium revenue rose from 38,627 to 43,052 in FY2025 while medical margin fell from 4,199 to 3,564 (10-K page:81). In 2026 premium revenue also fell (30,873 in 9M 2026 against 32,337), mainly on lower Medicaid and Marketplace membership (Q3 release page:1), so both a lower revenue base and a higher MCR now weigh on earnings. Marketplace MCR was 90.6% in FY2025 against 75.4% in FY2024 (10-K page:85).

- The fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss on a derived basis: FY2025 operating income of 781 less 9M 2025 of 943 gives -162 (see Calculations). That quarter is what lifts the LTM interest-cover measure down to 1.56x.

- Leverage view by balance sheet: debt to capital on a simple basis (debt over debt plus equity) is 47.58% at September 30, 2026, against 48.07% at December 31, 2025 and 39.40% at December 31, 2024. The covenant maximum is 60% (65% for four quarters after a material acquisition), defined by the credit agreement; the simple ratio is indicative only.

- Claims outside debt: medical claims and benefits payable of 4,988 and amounts due government agencies of 1,141 at September 30, 2026 are operating liabilities outside the debt figure (10-Q Q3 page:2). Finance lease liabilities were 209 in total at December 31, 2025 (25 current, 184 non-current) and operating lease liabilities 71 (10-K page:127); both are outside the debt figure. Pensions, factoring and supply-chain finance: none found in the sources (searched).

- Liquidity depends on subsidiary dividends: regulated subsidiaries paid 985 in 2025 and 997 in 2024 to the parent (10-K page:90); for 9M 2026 the parent received 329 in dividends and return of capital and contributed 130 of capital (10-Q Q3 page:35). Dividends payable without regulatory approval were about 170 in aggregate at December 31, 2025, and the company expected a decline in such dividends for 2026 (10-K page:94). Minimum statutory capital and surplus was about 3.1 billion at December 31, 2025 (10-K page:93).

- Capital return and financing: 1,000 of common stock was purchased in FY2025 and none in 9M 2026; 500 remained authorized through December 31, 2026 as of October 16, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:40). In FY2025 the company borrowed 1,100 under the credit facility and term loans and repaid 1,100, and issued the 850 6.500% notes in November 2025 with net proceeds of 838 (10-K page:107).

- Latest quarter and subsequent events to the cutoff: the Q3 release reaffirmed FY2026 guidance (premium revenue of approximately $42 billion; GAAP earnings of at least $2.38 per diluted share; adjusted earnings of at least $5.25), including a loss of $1.50 per share from implementing the new Florida Medicaid contract in Q4 2026 and $1.00 from traditional MAPD (Q3 release page:2). The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:18). The Q3 2026 debt note (10-Q Q3 pages 14-15) shows the same five notes as December 31, 2025 and no drawing on the revolver; no debt issuance or further amendment after February 4, 2026 appears in the pinned sources.

- Covenant facts: minimum interest coverage 3.0 to 1.0, reduced by the February 4, 2026 amendment to 1.75 to 1.00 for quarters ending March 31, 2026 to December 31, 2026, then 2.00 (March 2027), 2.50 (June 2027) and 2.75 (September 2027); maximum Consolidated Total Debt to Capital Ratio 60% (10-Q Q3 page:15). Compliance at September 30, 2026 is stated. The step-up of the floor in 2027 to 2.75 is a forward test; at the LTM September 2026 simple measure of 1.56x that is a material sensitivity if earnings do not recover.

### Business and transaction view

Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a listed, sponsor-free managed-care organisation that "provides managed healthcare services under the Medicaid and Medicare programs, and through the state insurance marketplaces" (10-K, page:108), operating in 21 states with about 4.9 million members at September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3, page:5). Its customers are government payers ("Our primary customers are state Medicaid agencies and the federal government", 10-Q Q3, page:31), so revenue is a fixed per-member-per-month premium that the health plan underwrites against medical cost, and the credit mechanism is the gap between rate updates (set annually by states and CMS) and medical cost trend. That gap is the central fact of the period: the 10-K describes a "rate and trend imbalance that we believe to be temporary" (page:86), the medical care ratio rose from 89.1% in FY2024 to 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in 9M 2026 (CP-1), and earnings compressed accordingly (CP-1 operating income, EBITDA and leverage). The business is concentrated: Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue (page:15), four state contracts (California, New York, Texas, Washington) each exceed 10% of Medicaid premium revenue, and Medicaid contracts run three to five years with either side able to terminate with or without cause (page:108), so each re-procurement is a revenue-durability event (Virginia was lost: contracts terminated June 30, 2025, page:12). Two portfolio actions are reshaping 2026 and 2027: the Marketplace book is being cut deliberately (9M 2026 Marketplace premium revenue 1,994 against 3,401, membership 267,000 against 713,000, 10-Q Q3 pages 31-34) and the traditional Medicare Advantage-Part D product will be exited for 2027 with a 93 impairment recognized in Q1 2026 (CP-1). Management's long-term growth targets (premium revenue growth of 11% to 13% and passing $50 billion in 2027, 10-K page:10) are Management Language and sit against FY2026 premium revenue guidance of approximately $42 billion, so they are not used as a base case. No sponsor, controlling holder, dividend recapitalisation or related-party leakage appears in the sources; the documented capital-allocation behaviour is a pattern of share repurchases funded by subsidiary dividends, assessed below as Neutral or Mixed. Debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes plus an undrawn revolver (CP-1); whether subsidiaries guarantee the notes is not stated in the sources. The evidence supports a business and transaction read at the level of Documentary Facts; it restricts conclusions on ownership, control rights and covenant capacity because the proxy-based ownership information and executed documents are not supplied.

spans.text: ## Request

As of 2026-11-05, this credit snapshot gives the fundamental credit view of MOLINA HEALTHCARE, INC. It synthesises the financial base and the business and transaction fact pack from the upstream modules only, in USD, for Q3 2026 against FY2025 and FY2024. It gives no peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion.
## Sources
### Issuer sources relied on (through the upstream handoffs; not re-read for this module)
| Source (exact name) | sha256 |

The context file (sha256 038deefd3d0187dee809d7ec7eb3f32548cc8a768b8a64a8e4dfbffc4bec802f) holds run settings only; its ratings, sponsor, guarantor and deal-term fields are blank and are not treated as zero.
### Supplied handoffs
| Module | sha256 | Use |
| CP-0 | 9a38b7e81c8a9d34c66cf8ba2d88f056039593cb8ea14bd1234abdea53036afb | Source readiness and gap list |
| CP-1 | 9d11362d7487441f85b5fd6c0bd9f2e0a792068fa4a098f857b8fd19f913a548 | Financial base: statements, calculated EBITDA, leverage, cover, liquidity, maturities |
| CP-1A | 8d68d07dfafdd70da9d54e48afe9785e45525c1897cc7d7694eaa7818533d333 | Business, transaction, governance, conflicts and timeline |
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Molina is a deteriorating credit with adequate near-term liquidity: debt of USD 3,771 million is 11.32x EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against 1.54x in FY2024, with no principal due before June 2028. | Medium | Covenant headroom cannot be verified because the covenant definitions and reported ratios are not supplied, and EBITDA is calculated rather than reported. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Operating income fell from USD 1,707 million in FY2024 to USD 781 million in FY2025 and to a calculated USD 172 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026. | Debt service rests on a thin earnings base, so small changes in medical costs move leverage and coverage sharply. | High |

| Simple EBITDA over interest expense is 1.56x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against a coverage floor of 1.75 to 1.00 stepping up to 2.75 by September 2027. | Headroom is unverifiable and the earnings recovery required grows through 2027, making covenant risk the main near-term uncertainty. | Low |

| No principal is due before USD 800 million in June 2028, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn, and parent cash and investments are USD 608 million. | Near-term refinancing risk is low, but parent liquidity depends on subsidiary dividends and statutory capital needs. | Medium |

| Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue and four state contracts are about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue; management expects 2026 to be the trough year for margins. | Recovery depends on rate updates catching up with medical costs, which is unproven, and state-specific events can be material. | Medium |
### Credit view

Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a deteriorating credit with adequate near-term liquidity: debt of USD 3,771 million equals 11.32x EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against 1.54x in FY2024 [CP-1 leverage table]. The strongest support is structure and timing: the debt is parent-level senior unsecured notes, no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028, and the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn. The weakest point is earnings: the medical care ratio reached 92.1% in nine months 2026 against 90.8%, leaving LTM EBITDA of USD 333 million against interest expense of USD 213 million. The outcome depends on whether Medicaid rate updates restore margins before the interest coverage floor steps up in 2027, which the sources cannot confirm.
### Key findings

The first finding is the speed of the earnings decline. Operating income fell from USD 1,707 million in FY2024 to USD 781 million in FY2025 and to a calculated USD 172 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, while debt stayed near USD 3,771 million, so calculated EBITDA of USD 1,893 million, USD 976 million and USD 333 million puts total debt at 1.54x, 3.86x and 11.32x [CP-1 financials table]. The mechanism is a fixed premium rate set against a medical cost trend that outran it: the medical care ratio was 89.1% in FY2024, 91.7% in FY2025 and 92.1% in nine months 2026, and the implied fourth quarter of 2025 was an operating loss of USD 162 million [CP-1 calculations]. Because debt did not fall, each point of margin lost translates directly into higher leverage. On the parent cash basis net debt is 9.50x EBITDA for the same twelve months. This is a calculated, Documentary Fact finding with high confidence in the inputs and medium confidence in the EBITDA definition, since the company reports no EBITDA.

The second finding is that covenant headroom, the question that matters most for creditors, cannot be measured. The credit agreement requires minimum interest coverage, which the February 4, 2026 amendment reduced from 3.0 to 1.0 to 1.75 to 1.00 through December 31, 2026, then 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 for the March, June and September 2027 quarters, and a maximum debt to capital ratio of 60%; the company states compliance at September 30, 2026 [CP-1 observations]. A simple EBITDA over interest expense measure is 1.56x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, or 2.00x with the USD 93 million non-cash impairment added back, but the agreement defines the ratio and that definition and the reported ratio are not supplied. The mechanism is that relief was taken in advance and the floor rises as the amendment expires; the implication is that earnings must recover materially during 2027 or relief must be extended, and a simple-basis shortfall is illustrated under Calculations. Confidence is low because the decisive figure is absent.

The third finding is that liquidity is adequate for debt service but sits at the parent. Consolidated cash and cash equivalents were USD 4,479 million at September 30, 2026, yet most of it supports claims and statutory capital at regulated health plans; parent cash and investments were USD 608 million against USD 223 million at December 31, 2025, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn, and no principal falls due before USD 800 million in June 2028 [CP-1 liquidity and maturity tables]. Subsidiary dividends to the parent were USD 985 million in 2025 and the parent received USD 329 million of dividends and return of capital in nine months 2026, against an expected decline in dividends payable without approval [CP-1 observations]. The mechanism is that creditors rely on subsidiary distributions that fall when earnings fall and that the parent must fund statutory capital first, so the revolver is the real backstop; letters of credit drawn on it are not printed, so availability net of letters of credit is unconfirmed.

The fourth finding is the maturity and refinancing profile. The five senior notes total USD 3,800 million in principal: USD 800 million in 2028, USD 650 million in 2030, USD 850 million in 2031, USD 750 million in 2032 and USD 750 million in 2033, at an annual coupon of about USD 191.4 million, or 5.04% of principal. Recent issuance priced at 6.500% in November 2025 and 6.250% in November 2024, so any refinancing at current levels raises cost, while LTM interest expense of USD 213 million already consumes a large share of the USD 333 million of EBITDA. The implication is limited near-term refinancing pressure but little capacity to absorb a further earnings shock before 2028.

The fifth finding concerns business risk. Medicaid is 75% of FY2025 premium revenue and four state contracts (California, New York, Texas and Washington) are about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue [CP-1A operating model]. Medicaid contracts run three to five years and either party may terminate, so re-procurement outcomes and annual rate setting drive revenue, and the Virginia contract loss shows the exposure. Management states that 2026 is the trough year for Medicaid margins and that recent rate updates are strong for 2027, which is Management Language that the results through the third quarter of 2026 do not yet support: the Medicaid medical care ratio was 93.0% in the third quarter against 92.0%. The sixth finding is that near-term earnings carry identified drags: guidance includes a loss of USD 1.50 per diluted share from the new Florida contract and a loss of USD 1.00 per diluted share from the Medicare product to be exited for 2027, and the GAAP guidance floor of USD 122 million net income implies only about USD 10 million for the fourth quarter. The sources conflict on the scale of the Florida contract (about 120,000 enrollees against USD 6 billion of annual premium revenue), so the size of that start-up cost cannot be verified [CP-1A conflicts].

The seventh finding is capital allocation and governance. The company repurchased USD 1,000 million of stock in FY2025, paused repurchases in nine months 2026 and retains USD 500 million of authorization through December 31, 2026, which is an Analyst Interpretation of Neutral or Mixed behaviour: the pause is supportive, but the authorization is a possible call on parent cash. The securities class action was dismissed with prejudice on October 20, 2026 and the derivative dismissal notice was filed on October 6, 2026, which removes an overhang. The only rating evidence is BB from S&P and Ba2 from Moody's as stated in the annual report.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. The first strength is a favourable maturity and liquidity structure: no principal is due before USD 800 million in June 2028, the USD 1,250 million revolver is undrawn and runs to November 20, 2030, and parent cash and investments rose to USD 608 million from USD 223 million, so the debt can be serviced for some time even on thin earnings (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The second is an unsecured, single-issuer capital structure at the parent with no sponsor, no creditor-adverse transaction found and no dividend recapitalisation, which limits governance and structural-priming risk (Documentary Fact, CP-1A, with the caveat that indentures are not supplied). The third is an established government-programme franchise with recent state procurement wins and a large Medicaid base; the contract win record is a management claim and is tagged Management Language, but the wins themselves are documented (CP-1A). The fourth is the pause in share repurchases in nine months 2026 and the dismissal of the securities and derivative suits, which reduce competing calls on parent cash and a legal overhang (Documentary Fact, CP-1 and CP-1A). The fifth is that operating cash flow was positive in nine months 2026 at USD 629 million, giving an operating cash flow less capital expenditure figure of USD 535 million, although this reflects settlement timing (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1).

Weaknesses. The first weakness is leverage on collapsed earnings: 11.32x total debt to EBITDA for the twelve months to September 30, 2026 against 1.54x in FY2024, with a simple EBITDA over interest expense of 1.56x (Documentary Fact for inputs, calculated, CP-1). The second is unverifiable covenant headroom against a floor that rises from 1.75 to 1.00 to 2.75 to 1.00 by September 2027 (Insufficient Information on the executed definition and ratio; the relief obtained in advance is an Analyst Interpretation of limited headroom). The third is dependence on subsidiary dividends and on consolidated cash that is largely tied to statutory capital, so the headline net cash position does not measure parent debt-service capacity (Analyst Interpretation, CP-1). The fourth is concentration in Medicaid and in four states, with short and terminable contracts and an unproven margin recovery (Documentary Fact and Management Language, CP-1A). The fifth is settlement-driven cash flow: operating cash flow was an outflow of USD 535 million in FY2025 and an inflow of USD 629 million in nine months 2026, so cash conversion is volatile (Documentary Fact, CP-1). The sixth is the identified 2026 and 2027 earnings drags from the Florida start-up and the Medicare exit, together with policy risk from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with the Florida contract size in conflict across the sources (Documentary Fact and conflict, CP-1A).
### Credit assessment and thesis
| Element | Statement | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Assessment | Molina Healthcare, Inc. is a deteriorating credit with adequate near-term liquidity, on a thin and uncertain earnings base | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1 leverage, cover, liquidity and maturity tables; CP-1A operating model and credit translations |

| Thesis | The credit rests on a long-dated, undrawn-revolver capital structure that buys time, while debt service and covenant headroom depend on Medicaid margins recovering during 2027 | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | As above |
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Interest coverage floor rises through 2027 | Floor of 1.75 to 1.00 steps to 2.00, 2.50 and 2.75 while LTM earnings are depressed; executed definition not supplied | Possible covenant pressure or need for further relief; revolver access would be affected | Critical |

| Medical cost trend outruns rates | Fixed state and federal premium rates reset annually; Medicaid MCR 93.0% in the third quarter | Sustained margin pressure keeps leverage double-digit on LTM EBITDA | Critical |

| Parent liquidity depends on subsidiaries | Statutory capital and dividend limits; subsidiary earnings fall with margins | Lower dividends reduce debt-service cushion; revolver is the backstop | Material |

| State and product concentration | Medicaid 75% of premium revenue; four states about 54% of Medicaid premium revenue; terminable contracts | A contract loss or repricing removes premium while fixed costs and debt remain | Material |

| Near-term earnings drags | Florida start-up (USD 1.50 per share) and Medicare exit (USD 1.00 per share) in guidance; Florida scale conflict | Delays recovery and weakens visibility into 2027 | Material |

| Refinancing cost and distribution risk | Recent notes priced at 6.250% and 6.500%; USD 500 million repurchase authorization remains | Higher cost on refinancing from 2028; possible call on parent cash | Minor |
## Calculations
All amounts are USD millions unless stated. Inputs are CP-1 figures unless noted.
| Item | Inputs | Result |
| Annual coupon as a share of LTM EBITDA | Annual coupon 191.4 / LTM EBITDA 333 | 57.5% |
| Simple-basis EBITDA needed for the 1.75x floor on LTM interest expense | 1.75 x 213 | 372.75, a shortfall of 39.75 against LTM EBITDA 333 (illustrative; not the covenant definition) |
